title: Recording Time Honestly in Missouri CDS: What Counts as Medicaid Fraud
description: Every hour a CDS caregiver works is billed to Medicaid. Here's exactly what counts as Medicaid fraud in Missouri's Consumer Directed Services program, why "they told me to" isn't a defense, what to do when you're not sure, the consequences, and how honest mistakes and overpayments get fixed fairly.
end: Not sure? Call us before you guess.

parts.head: Recording time honestly: what counts as Medicaid fraud
parts.sub: So you never get caught by surprise
parts.text: Every hour a CDS caregiver works is billed to Medicaid. So recording time honestly isn't just good practice. It's the law. I'm Samantha with Caring Companions CDS. Here's exactly what counts as Medicaid fraud, so you never get caught by surprise.

parts.head: Bad intentions aren't required
parts.text: First, know this. If time or tasks are submitted that aren't accurate, that's Medicaid fraud, and it doesn't take bad intentions to count.

parts.head: Hours that didn't happen
parts.sub: Days not worked. Extra hours. Time recorded early.
parts.text: So what counts? Time for days you didn't work. More hours than you actually worked. And time recorded before the work happened.

parts.head: Tasks that weren't done, or aren't approved
parts.sub: Like yard work, pet care or home repair
parts.text: Tasks marked that you didn't complete. And time for tasks that aren't on the plan of care, like yard work, pet care, or home repair.

parts.head: Days they were away
parts.sub: Hospital, rehab or a facility: no time recorded
parts.text: Time for days the person you care for was in the hospital, in rehab, or in a facility. Even three days in the hospital means no time can be recorded for those days.

parts.head: Days you were away
parts.sub: Or time while working for someone else
parts.text: And time for days you were in the hospital, in rehab, or otherwise unavailable, or time while you were working for someone else.

parts.head: Nobody works under your name
parts.sub: Sick? They use their backup caregiver.
parts.text: Never let anyone else work, or clock in, under your name. Not your sister, not a friend, even if the person you care for agrees. If you're sick, call them, so they can use their backup caregiver.

parts.head: "They told me to" isn't a defense
parts.sub: They can't approve time you didn't work
parts.text: Here's the most important sentence. The consumer told me to, is not a defense. They direct how approved work is done, but they can't approve time you didn't work. If you're asked to clock in while they go to the store alone, the answer is no.

parts.head: Stop. Ask. Write it down. Call us.
parts.sub: Asking first beats fixing it later
parts.text: When you're not sure, take four steps. Stop. Ask what they need, kindly. Write down the date, the time, and what happened. And call us. Asking first is always easier than fixing it later.

parts.head: The consequences are serious
parts.sub: Lifetime loss of eligibility, charges, money taken back
parts.text: Here's why it matters. We're required to report suspected Medicaid fraud to the state. People who break these rules can lose Medicaid eligibility for life, and face criminal charges, fines, and prison. And money paid on inaccurate time is taken back from both the caregiver and the consumer.

parts.head: Honest mistakes get fixed
parts.sub: The EVV correction form. Fair overpayment rules.
parts.text: Honest mistakes are different. A missed clock-in gets fixed with a correction form. And if you're ever overpaid, it's corrected fairly. You get written notice and a chance to dispute it, and your pay is never reduced without your written OK, or due process.
Questions about your time? Call us at 417-218-2888, before you guess. I'm Samantha with Caring Companions CDS. Thanks for watching.
